intuition.title: Why limit the small-molecule ligand
intuition.summary: The stated rationale for substoichiometric TDPA is to leave some Cd available to bind nanotube oxygen groups. This competition is a qualitative design principle; no binding constant, ligand-coverage measurement or critical TDPA ratio is established.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: Why oxidation changes the growth sites
intuition.summary: Opening tips and etching outer-wall defects is proposed to create oxygen-rich nucleation sites. Figures 2a,d show relatively greater particle density near tips. The authors relate high tip reactivity to curvature and prior acid-etching studies. These interpretations explain the images and oxidation controls but do not quantitatively assign a chemical group to each attached particle or count the removed wall layers.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: pH-mediated nucleation and growth
intuition.summary: The authors propose that high initial pH rapidly ionizes H₂S, enabling many small CdS nuclei. Continued dissociation and precipitation release acidity, slow further growth and lead to the final acidic pH. The printed sulfur-ion notation is S⁻; it is retained as source wording rather than treated as a validated solution-speciation measurement.

intuition.title: Separate well thickness from well count
intuition.summary: System II increases the thickness of one HgS well; system III places an additional HgS well across a CdS barrier. Comparing these with system I probes how spatial separation changes carrier confinement and optical transitions. The actual paper tests one stated barrier thickness, rather than a systematic barrier-thickness series.

intuition.title: pH-mediated nucleation and growth
intuition.summary: The authors propose that high initial pH rapidly ionizes H₂S, enabling many small CdS nuclei. Continued dissociation and precipitation release acidity, slow further growth and lead to the final acidic pH. The printed sulfur-ion notation is S⁻; it is retained as source wording rather than treated as a validated solution-speciation measurement.

intuition.title: Why a different growth temperature for each core size?
intuition.summary: High temperature promotes core Ostwald ripening and broadens its size distribution; low temperature risks incomplete precursor decomposition or poorly crystalline ZnS. The authors select growth temperatures separately by seed size to balance these effects. Note 22 lists observed method choices but does not provide a kinetic law, validated optimum search or quantitative temperature-to-size prediction.

intuition.title: Why a different growth temperature for each core size?

intuition.title: Why slow precursor delivery and optical monitoring?
intuition.summary: Slow, steady dosing is chosen to favor heterogeneous growth on the existing CdSe seeds and limit homogeneous ZnSe nucleation. Increased UV absorption, preserved CdSe band edge, particle enlargement and the no-seed comparison support the authors’ overgrowth interpretation together. Absorption shifts serve as a practical probe of core integrity; none of these observations alone resolves a uniform shell or specifies a kinetic rate law.

intuition.title: Proposed sequential two-photon mechanism

intuition.title: Use annealing to promote diffusion and growth
intuition.summary: The 350 °C treatment relieves glass stress, whereas the 600 °C treatment promotes diffusion of Pb²⁺ and S²⁻ and nanocrystal growth. Increasing anneal duration correlates with redshift and larger inferred sizes. A diffusion coefficient, nucleation rate, activation energy or complete kinetic model is not measured.

intuition.title: Surface energy, strain and growth modes
intuition.summary: The discussion contrasts Frank–van der Merwe layer growth, Volmer–Weber islands and Stranski–Krastanov layer-then-island growth. Cited calculations put Ge(100) surface free energy about 30% below Si(100), favoring layer growth, while approximately 4% lattice mismatch increases strain and favors S–K growth. Cited UHV/CVD context describes a transition from layer growth below T₀ = 350 °C to S–K and/or V–W modes above it. These are rationale/background values, not alternative settings demonstrated for the two patterned variants.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: Structural and photophysical interpretations
intuition.summary: The authors connect phase, octahedral distortion and magnetic/electronic models to the different luminescence behavior. They discuss surface stabilization, d–d transitions, self-trapped excitons and possible defects, while leaving the exact microscopic mechanism unresolved. intuition.title: Nucleation, coarsening and oriented attachment
intuition.summary: The authors infer that all studied solutions exceed saturation because precipitation occurs. From rapid early change they assume concentration-independent supersaturation and mean nucleus size in dilute suspensions, then attribute later size differences to growth and coarsening. They propose Sn(OH)4 formation followed by polycondensation to SnO2, while the conclusion also uses ion-deposition language. Neither phrasing establishes measured solution speciation or resolves the Sn(II)-to-Sn(IV) oxidation pathway. Their collision model permits attachment of compatible faces, including imperfect coalescence. These hypotheses are distinguished from the microscopy observations and do not define atomistic trajectories.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: Parameters affecting assembly
intuition.summary: The authors identify nanocrystal size/shape uniformity, ligand coating, interparticle spacing, temperature and concentration as assembly variables. Increased concentration and additional heating support aggregation, while longer time is proposed to permit more ordered arrangements. These qualitative relationships are not a fitted optimization model.

intuition.title: Parameters affecting assembly
intuition.summary: The authors identify nanocrystal size/shape uniformity, ligand coating, interparticle spacing, temperature and concentration as assembly variables. Increased concentration and additional heating support aggregation, while longer time is proposed to permit more ordered arrangements. These qualitative relationships are not a fitted optimization model.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: Ligand, purification and phase interpretations
intuition.summary: The authors relate ligand balance and washing conditions to precursor availability, passivation, dissolution and nonradiative recombination. Their temperature-dependent phase and emission model uses cited bulk reference cells. These explanations remain author interpretations, separate from measured occupancies, atomic coordinates, device performance or independently reproduced mechanisms.

intuition.title: Ligand mechanism interpretation
intuition.summary: The authors associate excess OAm with protonated OAm+ replacing FA+ and disrupting the lattice, insufficient OA with reduced FA-oleate formation, and excess OA with hindered growth and dissolution in washing solvent. These are mechanistic explanations, not measured occupancies, solution structures or reaction stoichiometries.

intuition.title: Why use solution chemistry
intuition.summary: Solution processing is proposed to improve control of dopant speciation, provide scalable preparation and make nanocrystals processable building blocks. intuition.title: Why partially fluorinated thiol?
intuition.summary: CO₂ has low polarizability and weak dispersion interactions, so suitable CO₂-solvated tails are needed for steric stabilization. The thiol group binds the metal while the fluorinated segment interacts with CO₂. The source contrasts bound capping molecules with microemulsion surfactants that can permit irreversible aggregation during recovery. Fluoroacrylates, alkanes and ethers are cited examples of compatible surfactant classes, not additional reagents used here.

intuition.title: Arrested precipitation and surface passivation
intuition.summary: The synthesis combines precursor reduction, metal nucleation and growth with adsorption of thiolate ligands. Adsorbed chains provide a steric barrier and eventually arrest growth. The article frames this as a single CO₂-phase method, unlike the earlier water-in-CO₂ microemulsion examples cited in references 20 and 21.

intuition.title: Why partially fluorinated thiol?
intuition.summary: CO₂ has low polarizability and weak dispersion interactions, so suitable CO₂-solvated tails are needed for steric stabilization. The thiol group binds the metal while the fluorinated segment interacts with CO₂. The source contrasts bound capping molecules with microemulsion surfactants that can permit irreversible aggregation during recovery. Fluoroacrylates, alkanes and ethers are cited examples of compatible surfactant classes, not additional reagents used here.

intuition.title: Arrested precipitation and surface passivation
intuition.summary: The synthesis combines precursor reduction, metal nucleation and growth with adsorption of thiolate ligands. Adsorbed chains provide a steric barrier and eventually arrest growth. The article frames this as a single CO₂-phase method, unlike the earlier water-in-CO₂ microemulsion examples cited in references 20 and 21.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

intuition.title: Why partially fluorinated thiol?
intuition.summary: CO₂ has low polarizability and weak dispersion interactions, so suitable CO₂-solvated tails are needed for steric stabilization. The thiol group binds the metal while the fluorinated segment interacts with CO₂. The source contrasts bound capping molecules with microemulsion surfactants that can permit irreversible aggregation during recovery. Fluoroacrylates, alkanes and ethers are cited examples of compatible surfactant classes, not additional reagents used here.

intuition.title: Coordination and impurity-mediated formation
intuition.summary: The authors propose that aluminum dimers can connect with tetrahedrally coordinated zinc to nucleate spinel. At high M/OH, zinc recoordination may delay this process and favor AlOOH; at low M/OH, ZnO dissolution supplies zinc and may leave residual ZnO. Heating history changes impurity formation and consumption. These explanations are source interpretations, with the contradictory conclusion wording preserved.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.

figures.summary: The original graphical abstract summarizes the proposed coordination-dependent nucleation pathways. figures.title: Figure 5 · Author-proposed high/low M/OH formation pathways
figures.summary: This proposed formation pathway connects aluminum dimers to tetrahedral zinc. At high M/OH, zinc must recoordinate from an octahedral precursor, while at low M/OH it is released from ZnO. The drawing expresses a mechanistic interpretation and leaves protonation, rates and exact intermediates unresolved.

intuition.title: Why N-acylimidazoles?
intuition.summary: The paper describes Cd–thiolate clusters as sensitive to acid/base conditions, heat, oxidation and competing sulfur chemistry. It selects N-acylimidazoles, used for phenolic tyrosine tagging in reference 9, to transfer acyl groups under mild conditions. Successful short-time derivatization and failures under direct-acyl-chloride or prolonged treatment support a limited reaction window; they do not identify a complete kinetic mechanism.
intuition.scope: Source discussion; interpretation and cited context are distinguished in the text.
